title: Counting, whole numbers and place value

concepts.title: Natural numbers and zero
concepts.explain: Touch each object once as you count. The last number tells you how many objects there are. Here we use natural numbers 1, 2, 3, … . Whole numbers also include 0.
steps: Five shells and three shells make eight shells.
An empty collection has 0 objects. Zero is a number, not an empty answer.

practice.prompt: An empty basket contains how many mangoes?
Which is a whole number but is not a natural number in this course?
practice.solution: Our natural numbers start at 1; whole numbers start at 0.

concepts.remember: Zero is neither positive nor negative. There is no largest natural number.
teaching: Count one object at a time: 1, 2, 3 and so on are natural numbers. When there are no objects, the count is 0. Including zero gives the whole numbers. Both lists continue without end.

Each step right on a number line increases a whole number by 1. The successor of 9 is 10; its predecessor is 8. Zero has no predecessor among whole numbers. Move each object once when counting so nothing is missed or counted twice.

concepts.title: Tens, hundreds and thousands
concepts.explain: Ten ones can be exchanged for one ten. Ten tens make one hundred. The face value of a digit is the digit itself. Its place value depends on its position in the number.
steps: The digit 4 is in the tens place, so its place value is 40.
In 2,406, the zero keeps the tens place: 2,000 + 400 + 0 + 6.

practice.prompt: What is the place value of 7 in 3,752?
practice.solution: 7 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 7 × 100 = 700.

practice.prompt: Which number means 5 hundreds, 0 tens and 9 ones?

concepts.remember: Face value is the digit itself; place value depends on its position. In 3,752, the face value of 7 is 7, and its place value is 700.
teaching: Ten ones can be exchanged for one ten without changing the total. Ten tens make one hundred, and ten hundreds make one thousand. Moving a digit one place left makes its place value ten times as large.
In 4,072, the place values are 4,000 for 4, 0 for 0, 70 for 7 and 2 for 2. The zero holds the hundreds place. Thus 4,072 = 4,000 + 70 + 2. Removing the zero would give 472, a different number.

concepts.title: Compare and order whole numbers
concepts.explain: Compare the number of digits first. If two numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left until a pair of digits differs. On a number line, the number farther right is greater.

visual.caption: 7 is farther right than 4, so 7 > 4.

steps: 3,481 > 3,418: thousands and hundreds match; 8 tens is greater than 1 ten.
In ascending order, 907, 970 and 790 become 790, 907, 970.
999 is followed by 1,000: ten hundreds make one thousand.

practice.prompt: Which number comes just after 999?
Which is greatest?
practice.solution: Thousands match; compare hundreds, then tens.

concepts.remember: Ascending means smallest to largest. Descending means largest to smallest.
teaching: Compare the number of digits first, ignoring leading zeros. A four-digit whole number is greater than a three-digit whole number. If the lengths match, compare from the left until the first unequal digits.

For 5,399 and 5,406, the thousands match. The hundreds are 3 and 4, so 5,399 < 5,406. Later digits cannot change that decision. Ascending order means smallest to largest. In a story, identify whether you need the largest amount, the smallest or the difference.

test.prompt: What is the smallest whole number?
test.solution: Whole numbers begin with 0.

test.prompt: What is the place value of 8 in 4,836?
test.solution: 8 is in the hundreds place, so its place value is 8 hundreds = 800.

test.prompt: Write the number: 6 hundreds, 2 tens and 4 ones.

test.solution: Thousands and hundreds match; 8 tens is greater than 6 tens.
5,399 has fewer hundreds than 5,406.
One less means subtract 1: 10,000 − 1 = 9,999.
There are 5 thousands, 7 hundreds, 0 tens and 9 ones: 5,709.
One ten is 10. Divide 400 by 10 to get 40 tens.

test.prompt: A library labels books from 1 to 36. How many labels are used?
test.solution: Each natural number from 1 through 36 labels one book, giving 36 labels.

test.prompt: Which list is in ascending order?
test.solution: Ascending means smallest to largest. Compare hundreds first, then tens.

concepts.title: Join and compare groups
concepts.explain: Addition combines amounts. Subtraction can mean taking away, finding what is missing, or comparing two amounts. Draw the quantities before choosing the operation.
steps: Together: 8 + 5 = 13 stickers.
Difference: 8 − 5 = 3 stickers.
Dev needs 3 more to have the same number as Asha.

practice.prompt: Mira has 9 beads and receives 6 more. How many now?
A bag has 14 apples and another has 9. How many more are in the first?

concepts.remember: “More” does not always tell you to add. “How many more?” often asks for a difference.
teaching: Addition combines amounts: 12 books and 7 more give 12 + 7 = 19 books. Subtraction can mean taking away, finding a missing part or comparing amounts. A shelf with 19 books has 7 more than a shelf with 12.

Draw the amounts as bars. Two parts with a missing whole suggest addition. A whole and one known part suggest subtraction. Read the complete situation rather than choosing from one word: “I have 7 more than you; I have 19” asks for 19 − 7.

concepts.title: Addition with regrouping
concepts.explain: Keep ones under ones and tens under tens. When a column contains ten or more, exchange ten of that unit for one unit in the next column.
steps: Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5 ones and carry 1 ten.
Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 tens. Write 2 tens and carry 1 hundred.
Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. The sum is 425.

practice.prompt: A school buys 235 pencils and then 187 pencils. Find the total.

concepts.remember: A carried 1 means one ten, one hundred or another place-value unit—not always one single object.
teaching: Write ones below ones, tens below tens and hundreds below hundreds. Start at the right. If a column totals ten or more, exchange ten units for one unit in the next column. This is regrouping; the total value stays the same.
For 268 + 157, 8 + 7 = 15 ones: write 5 and carry 1 ten. Then 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 tens: write 2 and carry 1 hundred. Finally 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 hundreds, giving 425. An estimate near 430 checks the size.

concepts.title: Subtraction with regrouping
concepts.explain: Exchange a larger unit when a column does not contain enough. Regrouping changes how the number is written, but not its value.
steps: 502 is 5 hundreds, 0 tens and 2 ones.
Exchange: 4 hundreds, 9 tens and 12 ones still make 502.

practice.solution: Regroup 604 as 5 hundreds, 9 tens and 14 ones; subtract to get 318.

practice.prompt: You pay ₹500 for a ₹368 bag. What is the change?

concepts.remember: Subtract the lower number from the upper number in each column after regrouping; do not reverse individual digits.
teaching: Align the place-value columns. If a column has too few units to subtract, exchange one unit from the next column for ten smaller units. If that next column is zero, first exchange from a nonzero column farther left.
For 502 − 178, exchange to get 4 hundreds, 10 tens and 2 ones, then 4 hundreds, 9 tens and 12 ones. Subtract each column: 12 − 8 = 4, 9 − 7 = 2 and 4 − 1 = 3. Check: 324 + 178 = 502.

test.solution: Add with regrouping: 643.
Regroup through the zero; the difference is 245.

test.prompt: Two shelves hold 128 and 96 books. How many altogether?
A team scores 72; another scores 58. What is the difference?

test.solution: Ones: 6+5=11. Tens: 8+7+1=16. Hundreds: 4+1+1=6. The sum is 661.
Regroup 900 as 8 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones. Subtract each column: 533.

test.prompt: A bus has 47 passengers. 18 leave and 9 enter. How many are on the bus now?
test.solution: Subtract those leaving, then add those entering: 47−18+9=29+9=38.
Add the amount removed to the remainder: 289+156=445. Check: 445−156=289.

test.prompt: Mina has ₹275 and needs ₹430. How much more does she need?
test.solution: Find the difference: 430−275=155. Check: 275+155=430.

concepts.title: Equal groups and times tables
concepts.explain: Multiplication counts equal groups. Learn a table by building or splitting groups, not only by reciting it.

visual.caption: 4 rows of 6 counters: 4 × 6 = 24

steps: 4 × 6 and 6 × 4 both count 24 counters.

practice.prompt: There are 8 packets with 4 biscuits each. How many biscuits?
Find 9 × 7 using 10 × 7 − 7.

concepts.remember: Check the groups first: multiplication counts equal groups. Each row in our garden has the same number of flowers.
teaching: Picture 4 rows with 6 flowers in every row. Count along: 6, 12, 18, 24! Turn the arrangement and you have 6 rows of 4. Same flowers, same total: 4 × 6 = 6 × 4 = 24.

Want 7 rows of 6? Start with 5 rows: 30 flowers. Add 2 more rows: 12 flowers. Altogether, 30 + 12 = 42. One row keeps the group’s number; zero rows gives zero. If the rows have different numbers, count and add each row separately.

concepts.title: Multiply using place value
concepts.explain: Break a number into tens and ones. Each part must be multiplied. The written method is a shorter record of these partial products.
steps: For 36 × 24, split 24 into 20 + 4.
Add the partial products: 144 + 720 = 864.
Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800, so 864 is reasonable.

practice.prompt: Find 23 × 6.
Find 42 × 13.

concepts.remember: In the tens row, multiply by 20, not by 2. The place-value zero matters.
teaching: Split a multi-digit multiplier by place value. In 36 × 24, the 24 means 20 + 4, so calculate both 36 × 20 and 36 × 4, then add the partial products.

First 36 × 4 = 144. Next 36 × 20 = 720, because twenty is two tens. Adding gives 720 + 144 = 864. The zero in 720 records place value. Estimate 40 × 20 = 800 to check that the answer is a sensible size.

concepts.title: Sharing, grouping and remainders
concepts.explain: Division can share a total equally or count how many equal groups fit. A remainder is what is left after making complete groups.
steps: 16 counters shared among 4 groups gives 4 in each: 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
For 157 ÷ 6: 15 tens ÷ 6 gives 2 tens, with 3 tens left.
Bring down 7 ones: 37 ÷ 6 gives 6 ones, remainder 1. So 157 ÷ 6 = 26 remainder 1.
Check: 6 × 26 + 1 = 157. If 157 children need 6-seat vans, 27 vans are needed.

practice.prompt: 144 pencils are packed 12 per box. How many boxes?
29 children travel in cars with 4 child seats each. How many cars are needed?
practice.solution: 29 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 1. Seven cars leave one child, so use eight.

concepts.remember: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor. Division by zero is undefined.
teaching: Division shares a total equally or counts equal groups. Sharing 24 pencils among 6 children gives 4 each. Packing 24 pencils into groups of 6 gives 4 groups. Multiplication checks both: 6 × 4 = 24.

For 157 ÷ 6, 6 × 26 = 156, leaving 1. A remainder must be smaller than the divisor. If 157 people need six-seat vans, 26 vans leave one person behind, so 27 vans are needed. Interpret the remainder in the story.

test.prompt: What is the remainder when 95 is divided by 8?
A trip has 53 people and 10 seats per van. How many vans?
test.solution: Five vans seat 50, so a sixth is needed.
9×20=180 and 9×8=72. Together 180+72=252, so the quotient is 28.

test.prompt: Each packet holds 18 crayons. How many crayons are in 7 packets?
test.solution: Equal groups call for multiplication: 7×18=7×(10+8)=70+56=126.

test.prompt: What is the quotient when 173 is divided by 5, leaving a remainder?
test.solution: 5×34=170 and 173−170=3. The quotient is 34 and the remainder is 3.

test.prompt: A ribbon 96 cm long is cut into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece, in cm?
test.solution: Share the total equally: 96÷8=12. Check: 8×12=96.

concepts.title: What does an estimate tell us?
concepts.explain: An estimate is a sensible nearby value, not a guess with no reasoning. Use one when an exact count is unnecessary or to check a calculation. Choose a unit of rounding that suits the situation.

visual.caption: 198 is only 2 away from 200. It is 8 away from 190.

steps: A hall has 198 visitors. Saying “about 200” gives a useful idea of the crowd.
A bill of ₹198 must still be paid exactly; an estimate does not replace the bill.
For 198 + 303, nearby hundreds give 200 + 300 = about 500. The exact sum is 501.

practice.prompt: Which is a useful estimate of 398 people to the nearest hundred?
A bill is exactly ₹247. Does rounding it to ₹250 change the amount owed?
practice.solution: Rounding helps planning; the actual bill remains ₹247.

concepts.remember: An estimate should state its accuracy, such as “to the nearest ten”.
teaching: An estimate is a sensible nearby value when an exact count is difficult or unnecessary. Use ≈ for an approximation and = for exact equality. An estimate should be close enough for its purpose.

For 198 children, you might say about 200. But planning only 190 seats would leave children standing. Decide whether you are checking a calculation, planning supplies or describing a large amount before choosing how closely to estimate.

concepts.title: Round to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
concepts.explain: Find the two neighbouring multiples of the unit. Compare distances. Choose the nearer one. If exactly halfway, this course rounds a positive number up.

visual.caption: 347 is 7 from 340 and 3 from 350, so it rounds to 350.

steps: 347 to the nearest ten: neighbours 340 and 350; choose 350.
347 to the nearest hundred: neighbours 300 and 400; choose 300.
3,650 to the nearest hundred: exactly between 3,600 and 3,700; choose 3,700.
4,499 to the nearest thousand is 4,000. Compare directly with 4,500; do not round in several stages.

practice.prompt: Round 764 to the nearest ten.
Round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.
practice.solution: It is halfway, so round up to 2,700.

concepts.remember: The same number can round differently depending on the place requested.
teaching: To round 347 to the nearest ten, locate 340 and 350. Their distances from 347 are 7 and 3, so choose 350. At the midpoint, the usual school rule for positive numbers is to round up.

For 3,462 to the nearest hundred, compare with the midpoint 3,450 between 3,400 and 3,500: round to 3,500. To the nearest thousand, compare with 3,500 between 3,000 and 4,000: round to 3,000. Always identify the requested place.

concepts.title: Estimate sums and differences
concepts.explain: Round each quantity to the requested place, then calculate with the rounded numbers. Write “about” or ≈, not an exact equals sign. Mixed rounding may make an estimate too high or too low.
steps: For 287 + 412, round each to the nearest hundred: 300 + 400 = 700. Exact sum: 699.
For 824 − 391, nearest hundreds give 800 − 400 = 400. Exact difference: 433.
If small differences matter, use tens instead: 820 − 390 = about 430.

practice.prompt: Estimate 486 + 218 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred.
Estimate 763 − 326 by rounding each number to the nearest ten.

concepts.remember: Round the quantities as instructed before calculating. Rounding only the final exact answer is a different method.
teaching: Choose a rounding place that makes the calculation easy but keeps useful detail. For 398 + 207, use 400 + 200 = 600. The exact sum is 605. Rounding inputs can make the final estimate slightly larger or smaller.

For 504 − 496, rounding to hundreds gives 500 − 500 = 0 and hides the gap. Here the exact difference 8 is more useful. An estimation method should suit the question, rather than follow the same rounding rule every time.

concepts.title: Estimate products, quotients and check answers
concepts.explain: For multiplication use nearby easy numbers. For division choose compatible numbers that divide easily. Compare the estimate with the proposed answer to catch place-value errors.

rows: 7,980 is about ten times too large

steps: 19 × 42 is about 20 × 40 = 800. An answer of 7,980 cannot be reasonable.
To estimate 397 ÷ 8, use 400 ÷ 8 = 50. The exact result is slightly below 50.
For 6 items at ₹49 each, plan about 6 × ₹50 = ₹300. Actual cost ₹294.

practice.prompt: Estimate 29 × 61 by rounding each factor to the nearest ten.
Use 600 ÷ 6 to estimate 598 ÷ 6.
practice.solution: 600 ÷ 6 = 100; the exact answer is slightly less.

concepts.remember: Reasonable does not mean certainly correct. Check the exact calculation when accuracy is needed.
teaching: Use nearby easy factors for products: 49 × 21 ≈ 50 × 20 = 1,000. For division, choose compatible numbers: 398 ÷ 8 ≈ 400 ÷ 8 = 50. You do not need to round both numbers to the same place.

Compare an exact result with your estimate. An answer of 10,029 for 49 × 21 is far from 1,000 and signals an error; the correct product is 1,029. A close estimate helps check size but does not prove every digit is correct.

test.solution: 853 is closer to 850 than 860.
Halfway between 4,700 and 4,800: round up.
Compatible numbers: 420 ÷ 7 = 60.
The neighbouring hundreds are 6,300 and 6,400. The distances are 49 and 51, so choose 6,300.
8,501 is above the midpoint 8,500, so it rounds to 9,000.

test.prompt: Estimate 918 − 486 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred.
test.solution: Round 918 to 900 and 486 to 500, then subtract: 900−500=400.

test.prompt: Estimate 38 × 52 by rounding each factor to the nearest ten.
test.solution: 38 rounds to 40 and 52 rounds to 50. Multiply: 40×50=2,000.

test.prompt: A student says 21 × 39 = 8,190. Is the answer reasonable?
test.solution: 20×40=800 is a useful estimate. 8,190 is about ten times too large. The exact answer is 819.

concepts.title: Numbers on both sides of zero
concepts.explain: Positive and negative numbers describe opposite directions from a chosen zero: above or below sea level, gain or loss, or warmer or colder than 0°C.

visual.caption: −4 < 2 because −4 lies to the left of 2.

steps: −2 is greater than −5 because it is farther right.
The distance of −5 from zero is 5; this is its absolute value.

practice.prompt: Which is greater?
What is the distance of −7 from zero?

concepts.remember: A larger negative numeral can represent a smaller number: −90 < −9.
teaching: Negative numbers describe positions below a reference, such as temperatures below zero. Integers include negative whole numbers, zero and positive whole numbers. On the number line, values increase from left to right.

Zero is neither positive nor negative. The number −5 is smaller than −2 because it lies farther left. Opposites such as 4 and −4 are equally far from zero. Their distance from zero is called their absolute value.

concepts.title: Add and subtract integers
concepts.explain: On a number line, add a positive number by moving right and a negative number by moving left. Subtracting a number means adding its opposite.

visual.caption: Start at −3 and move 5 right: −3 + 5 = 2.

steps: −3 + 5 = 2: five rightward steps from −3.
4 + (−7) = −3: seven leftward steps from 4.
A temperature rises from −4°C by 9°C: −4 + 9 = 5°C.

practice.prompt: Find −8 + 13.

concepts.remember: For unlike signs in addition, compare magnitudes. Do not apply multiplication sign rules to addition.
teaching: Adding a positive integer moves right on the number line; adding a negative integer moves left. From −3, adding 5 reaches 2, while adding −5 reaches −8.

Subtraction means adding the opposite: 4 − (−3) = 4 + 3 = 7. With the same signs, add the sizes and keep the sign. With opposite signs, subtract the smaller size from the larger and use the sign of the number farther from zero.

concepts.title: Multiply and divide signed numbers
concepts.explain: Equal repeated losses give a negative total. The sign pattern for products extends consistently: same signs give a positive result; different signs give a negative result. Division uses the same sign pattern.

visual.caption: Each step reduces the first factor by 1; the product increases by 4.

steps: A loss of ₹6 on each of 5 days is 5 × (−6) = −30.
0 ÷ (−5) = 0, but (−5) ÷ 0 is undefined.

practice.solution: Two negative factors give a positive product: 36.
Different signs give a negative quotient: −9.

concepts.remember: “Two negatives make a positive” applies to multiplication and division, not to −4 + (−3).
teaching: First multiply the positive sizes, then decide the sign. One negative factor gives a negative product; two negative factors give a positive product. Four groups of a loss of three give 4 × (−3) = −12.

In the pattern 2 × (−3) = −6, 1 × (−3) = −3 and 0 × (−3) = 0, the results increase by 3 each step. The next is (−1) × (−3) = 3. Division follows the same sign pattern because it reverses multiplication. Division by zero is undefined.

test.solution: The leftmost number is −12.
14 negative units and 9 positive units leave 5 negative units.
Different signs: −56.

test.prompt: At −3°C, temperature falls by 8°C. Find the new temperature.

test.solution: The signs are the same, so the result is positive. 63÷9=7.
Subtracting 7 moves 7 places left from −12: −19.
A number and its opposite have sum zero.

test.prompt: An elevator moves from floor −2 to floor 5. How many floors does it rise?
test.solution: From −2 to 0 is 2 floors and from 0 to 5 is 5 more: 2+5=7.
−4 lies to the right of −9 on a number line.

concepts.title: Equal priority: work from left to right
concepts.explain: Multiplication and division have equal priority. Addition and subtraction have equal priority. Do the multiplication/division stage first, then the addition/subtraction stage.

visual.caption: Division comes first here because it is farther left—not because D always beats M.

concepts.remember: DMAS does not mean “do every division before every multiplication.”
teaching: Multiplication and division have equal priority: work left to right. Then do addition and subtraction left to right. DMAS does not mean division always comes before multiplication or addition before subtraction.
For 24 ÷ 6 × 2, calculate 4 × 2 = 8. For 18 − 5 + 2, calculate 13 + 2 = 15. Rewrite the remaining expression at each step so you do not lose a term.

concepts.title: Brackets and a story calculation
concepts.explain: Brackets group an amount that must be calculated first. If powers occur, evaluate them after brackets and before multiplication/division.

visual.caption: Three packs contain 8 red and 2 blue pens each; 4 pens are used.

steps: Each pack contains 8 + 2 = 10 pens.
Three packs contain 3 × 10 = 30 pens.
After using 4, there are 30 − 4 = 26 pens.
Compare 2 × 3² = 18 with (2 × 3)² = 36.

practice.prompt: Find 4 + 2³ × 3.

concepts.remember: Read the story before writing an expression. Brackets must represent the intended groups.
teaching: Do brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. For nested brackets, start with the innermost group.

In 3 × (8 + 2) − 4, first add to get 10, multiply to get 30, then subtract to get 26. This can represent three packs of eight pencils and two pens, with four items given away. Brackets keep the contents of each pack together.

test.solution: Multiply first: 6 + 35 = 41.

test.prompt: Five boxes have 6 pencils each; 8 pencils are given away. How many remain?

test.solution: Complete division and multiplication first: 6+15=21.
Divide first: 12÷3=4. Then 30−4=26.
Brackets: 9−2=7. Multiply: 4×7=28. Add: 28+6=34.
Equal-priority divisions go left to right: 36÷3=12, then 12÷2=6.

test.prompt: Three packets contain 12 biscuits each. Two children each eat 5 biscuits. How many remain?
test.solution: Start with 3×12=36 biscuits. Subtract 2×5=10 eaten: 36−10=26.

concepts.title: Factors make exact rectangles
concepts.explain: A positive factor divides a positive whole number without a remainder. Find factor pairs by arranging all the counters into complete rectangular arrays.
steps: The positive factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.
4 is not a factor: 18 ÷ 4 leaves a remainder.

practice.prompt: How many positive factors does 10 have?
Which is a factor of 28?

concepts.remember: List both numbers in every factor pair, but count a repeated factor only once.
teaching: A factor divides a whole number exactly, leaving no remainder. Arrange 18 counters in complete equal rows: 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6. Each rectangle names a factor pair.

The factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. Stop when pairs repeat in reverse. A positive whole number has finitely many factors, each at most the number itself. In packing problems, a factor gives a group size with no leftovers.

concepts.title: Multiples and divisibility
concepts.explain: Multiples are obtained by multiplying by whole numbers. Positive multiples keep going forever. Divisibility rules help you test for factors.
steps: Positive multiples of 7 are 7, 14, 21, 28, … . Zero is also a multiple of 7.
Divisible by 2: even last digit; by 5: last digit 0 or 5; by 10: last digit 0.
For 3 or 9, add the digits. 351 has digit sum 9, so it is divisible by both 3 and 9.
For 4, check the last two digits: 516 is divisible by 4 because 16 is.

practice.prompt: What is the sixth positive multiple of 7?
Which number is divisible by 9?

concepts.remember: A factor fits into a number. A multiple is made by multiplying that number.
teaching: Multiples are totals made from equal groups: 7, 14, 21 and 28 are positive multiples of 7. Factors divide a number; multiples are made by multiplying it. Thus 7 is a factor of 21 and 21 is a multiple of 7.

An even last digit means divisibility by 2; a final 0 or 5 means divisibility by 5. For 3 or 9, test the digit sum; for 4, test the last two digits. Since 324 has digit sum 9 and last two digits 24, it is divisible by 3, 9 and 4.

concepts.title: Prime and composite numbers
concepts.explain: A prime is a positive whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors. A composite number has more than two.
steps: 13 has only 1 and 13 as factors, so it is prime.
15 has 1, 3, 5 and 15, so it is composite.
1 has only one positive factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
2 is the only even prime.

practice.prompt: Which is prime?
How many positive factors does a prime number have?

concepts.remember: Odd does not mean prime: 9, 15 and 21 are odd composite numbers.
teaching: A prime has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself. A composite has more than two. The number 13 cannot form a rectangle with both sides greater than 1, whereas 15 = 3 × 5 can.

The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. The number 2 is the only even prime, because larger even numbers have 2 as an extra factor. To test a larger number, try prime divisors up to its square root: any larger factor must have a smaller partner.

test.prompt: What is the fifth positive multiple of 9?

test.solution: 1 has only one factor.
Its last two digits, 32, are divisible by 4.

test.prompt: How many positive factors does 16 have?
How many positive factors does 20 have?
test.solution: Pair the factors: 1×20, 2×10 and 4×5. The six factors are 1,2,4,5,10,20.

test.prompt: What is the seventh positive multiple of 6?
test.solution: The nth positive multiple is the number multiplied by n: 6×7=42.
29 has only 1 and 29 as positive factors. The other options have additional factors.
Its digit sum is 4+3+2=9. Since 9 is divisible by 9, so is 432.

test.prompt: A teacher arranges 28 counters in equal rows of 4. How many rows are made?
test.solution: 4 is a factor of 28 because 4×7=28. There are 7 rows.

concepts.title: Prime factorisation
concepts.explain: Break a composite number into factors until every factor is prime. Different factor trees lead to the same prime factors, apart from order.

practice.prompt: What is the missing prime in 42 = 2 × 3 × □?
How many factors of 2 appear in the prime factorisation of 40?

concepts.remember: The leaves of a completed prime factor tree must all be prime; 1 is not a prime factor.
teaching: Prime factorisation writes an integer greater than 1 as a product of primes. Start with any factor pair, split each composite factor again, and stop when every branch of the factor tree is prime.
For 60, one route is 6 × 10 = 2 × 3 × 2 × 5, so 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. Different trees give the same prime factors in a different order. Keep repeated factors and multiply them back to check.

concepts.title: HCF: largest equal groups or lengths
concepts.explain: The highest common factor is the greatest positive number that divides all the given numbers. Use it when something must fit exactly into each amount.

visual.caption: 24 cm and 36 cm ribbons cut into the longest equal pieces: 12 cm.

steps: The largest common factor is 12. Cut 2 pieces from 24 cm and 3 from 36 cm.
With prime factors, keep only common primes, using the smaller power.

practice.prompt: Find the HCF of 14 and 35.
practice.solution: Common factors are 1 and 7; the greatest is 7.

practice.prompt: 20 red and 30 blue beads form the greatest possible number of identical packets, with none left. How many packets?
practice.solution: HCF(20,30)=10. Each packet has 2 red and 3 blue beads.

concepts.remember: In the bead problem, HCF gives the number of packets—not the total beads per packet.
teaching: The highest common factor is the largest number dividing all given numbers exactly. Use it when cutting different quantities into the largest equal parts with nothing left over. Each part must divide every quantity.

For 24 cm and 36 cm ribbons, 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Keep only the shared prime copies: 2² × 3 = 12. Pieces of 12 cm give two pieces from one ribbon and three from the other. Extra prime copies would fail to divide one ribbon.

concepts.title: LCM: first shared repeat
concepts.explain: The least common multiple is the smallest positive number that is a multiple of all the given numbers. Use it for events repeating together or the smallest common total.
steps: A bell rings every 4 minutes; another every 6 minutes. They ring together now.
Their positive common multiples start at 12, then 24. They next ring together after 12 minutes.
With prime factors, use every prime needed, taking the larger power.
HCF divides into both amounts; LCM is divisible by both amounts.

practice.prompt: Find the LCM of 6 and 15.
Two lights flash every 8 and 12 seconds, together now. After how many seconds do they next flash together?
practice.solution: The first common positive multiple of 8 and 12 is 24.

concepts.remember: The word “greatest” or “smallest” alone is not enough. Decide whether you need a common divisor or a common multiple.
teaching: The least common multiple is the smallest positive multiple shared by all given numbers. Use it for the first time repeating events coincide or the smallest equal total made from different pack sizes.

For bells ringing every 4 and 6 minutes, use 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 × 3. Keep enough prime copies for both: 2² × 3 = 12. The first common time is 12 minutes. HCF uses shared copies; LCM uses the greatest required power of each prime.

test.solution: 18=2×3² and 42=2×3×7; common product 2×3=6.
Use 2²×3²=36.

test.prompt: 32 and 48 sweets must form the greatest number of identical gift bags. How many bags?
test.solution: HCF(32,48)=16; each has 2 of one kind and 3 of the other.

test.prompt: Two buses depart every 10 and 15 minutes, together at 9:00. How many minutes until their next shared departure?
test.solution: LCM(10,15)=30, so the time is 9:30.

test.prompt: What is the missing factor in 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × □?

test.solution: 28=2×2×7 and 42=2×3×7. The common prime factors give 2×7=14.
8=2³ and 14=2×7. Use the highest power of each prime: 2³×7=56.

test.prompt: Ribbons of 45 cm and 60 cm are cut into the longest possible equal pieces with no waste. Find each piece length, in cm.
test.solution: The length must divide both 45 and 60. Their HCF is 15, so each piece is 15 cm long.

test.prompt: Two lights flash every 6 and 15 seconds. Starting together, after how many seconds do they next flash together?
test.solution: Use the LCM of 6 and 15. Multiples first coincide at 30 seconds.

test.prompt: Find the HCF of the prime numbers 11 and 17.
test.solution: Distinct primes have no common factor greater than 1, so their HCF is 1.

concepts.title: Equal parts and equivalent fractions
concepts.explain: A fraction compares selected equal parts with the whole. The denominator counts equal parts in the whole; the numerator counts parts selected.
steps: 3 shaded parts out of 8 equal parts represent 3/8.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number keeps the value: 3/8 = 6/16.

practice.prompt: What is the missing numerator: $\frac{2}{5}=\frac{\square}{20}$?
practice.solution: Multiply both numerator and denominator by 4.

practice.prompt: Write the numerator when 3¼ is written as an improper fraction.

concepts.remember: Equal parts must be equal in size, not merely equal in number.
teaching: The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts the chosen parts. In 3/8, three of eight equal parts are selected. Unequal pieces cannot be counted as equal eighths.

Splitting each part in two gives 3/8 = 6/16 without changing the amount. Multiply or divide both parts of a fraction by the same nonzero number. For 11/4, division gives two wholes and three quarters, so 11/4 = 2¾.

concepts.title: Calculate with fractions
concepts.explain: For addition or subtraction, first use equal-sized parts. For multiplication, multiply numerators and denominators. Division by a nonzero fraction multiplies by its reciprocal.
steps: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8 = 6: six eighths fit in three quarters.

practice.prompt: What is the numerator of 2/7 + 3/7 in simplest form?
How many quarter-litre cups fill 2 litres?

concepts.remember: Do not add denominators: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5, not 3/10.
teaching: For addition and subtraction, first make the piece sizes equal using a common denominator. For 1/3 + 1/4, use twelfths: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12. Add numerators while keeping the denominator.

Multiplication finds a part of a part: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5. Division asks how many portions fit: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6 because three quarters contain six eighths. Multiplying by the reciprocal performs this division. Never divide by zero.

test.solution: Divide both by 3.
Use sixths: 3/6+2/6.
Find one fifth first, then take three such parts: 25÷5×3=15.

test.prompt: How many halves fit in 5 wholes?

test.solution: Divide the numerator and denominator by their HCF, 7.
The parts have the same size, so add the numerators and keep denominator 7.
Multiply: 6/12. Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 6.
Multiply by the reciprocal: 2/5×10=20/5=4.

test.prompt: A 32-page booklet has 3/8 of its pages illustrated. How many pages are illustrated?
test.solution: One eighth is 32÷8=4 pages. Three eighths is 3×4=12 pages.

concepts.title: Tenths and hundredths
concepts.explain: A decimal extends place value to parts smaller than one. Ten hundredths make one tenth. Trailing zeros after the decimal point do not change the value.
steps: 37 shaded squares out of 100 represent 0.37.
0.6 = 0.60 > 0.57. Compare equal place-value columns.

practice.prompt: How many hundredths are in 0.45?
Which is larger?

concepts.remember: More decimal digits do not necessarily mean a larger number.
teaching: Decimal places continue place value to the right of ones: tenths, hundredths, then thousandths. Thus 0.37 = 3/10 + 7/100 = 37/100. These digits represent parts of one whole.
Trailing decimal zeros do not change value: 0.5 = 0.50. Compare 0.50 with 0.37 by tenths, then hundredths. Do not compare the digits 5 and 37 as though both were whole numbers.

concepts.title: Decimal operations
concepts.explain: Line up decimal points to add or subtract. For multiplication, count the total decimal places. For division, scale both numbers by the same power of ten if the divisor is a decimal.
steps: 3.6 × 0.4 = 1.44 because 36×4=144 and there are two decimal places.
concepts.remember: Only scale both dividend and divisor by the same amount; scaling just one changes the answer.
teaching: For addition and subtraction, align decimal points so equal place values meet. Add trailing zeros when helpful: 12.5 + 7.75 becomes 12.50 + 7.75 = 20.25.
For 3.6 × 0.4, calculate 36 × 4 = 144 and account for two decimal places to get 1.44. For division, scale both quantities equally: 4.8 ÷ 0.6 = 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Estimate to check the decimal point.

test.solution: 4 tenths + 8 hundredths = 48 hundredths.
15×2=30 with two decimal places: 0.30.
Multiply both dividend and divisor by ten to make the divisor whole: 63÷7=9.

test.prompt: Four pens cost ₹8.50 each. Find the total cost.
test.solution: Multiply the price of one pen by the number of pens: 4×8.50=34.
Write 2.6 as 2.60, align decimal points, and add: 4.75+2.60=7.35.
Write 8 as 8.00. Subtract with aligned decimal places: 8.00−2.37=5.63.
7×8=56. The factors have two decimal places altogether, giving 0.56.
Multiply both numbers by 10: 72÷9=8. The quotient is unchanged.

test.prompt: A jug contains 2.5 litres. After pouring out 0.85 litres, how many litres remain?
test.solution: Subtract the amount poured: 2.50−0.85=1.65 litres.

concepts.title: Compare parts and find one unit
concepts.explain: A ratio compares quantities in the stated order. A rate compares different units, such as rupees per kilogram. Convert to the same units before forming a ratio of like quantities.
steps: Red : blue = 3 : 5. Red : all = 3 : 8.
If 4 notebooks cost ₹72, one costs 72÷4=₹18.
Seven notebooks cost 7×18=₹126.

practice.prompt: Simplify 12:18.
5 kg rice costs ₹240. What is the cost per kg?

concepts.remember: A part-to-part ratio is not a fraction of the whole.
teaching: A red-to-blue ratio of 3:5 means three equal shares of red for every five of blue. There are eight shares altogether, not five. The order of the named quantities matters.

For 40 counters, each share is 40 ÷ 8 = 5. Red gets 15 and blue gets 25. Convert measurements to the same unit before making a ratio. For a constant price rate, find the price of one item, then multiply.

concepts.title: Direct and inverse proportion
concepts.explain: In direct proportion, the ratio stays constant. In inverse proportion, the product stays constant. Use these models only when the stated conditions stay the same.

visual.caption: Cost = 9 × number of pens

steps: At the same price, twice as many pens cost twice as much.
For a fixed job, twice as many equally productive workers take half as long, assuming they do not hinder each other.
6 workers × 8 days = 48 worker-days; 12 workers need 48÷12=4 days.

practice.prompt: At ₹15 each, what do 6 pens cost?
4 identical taps fill a tank in 12 minutes. How long would 8 taps take under the same conditions?

concepts.remember: Not every relationship is proportional. A taxi with a fixed starting charge is one counterexample.
teaching: In direct proportion, doubling one quantity doubles the other because the rate stays fixed. If four notebooks cost 60 rupees, one costs 15 and seven cost 105. Cost divided by count stays constant.

In inverse proportion, the product stays constant. For a fixed job and equally fast workers, twice as many workers take half the time, assuming they can work together without delay. Identify what stays fixed before choosing the model.

test.solution: Divide both by 5.

test.prompt: 3 metres cost ₹96. What do 5 metres cost?
A 2:7 ratio has how many parts altogether?
test.solution: Add the shares in both parts of the ratio: 2+7=9.

test.prompt: 5 equally productive workers finish in 18 days. How many days for 10?
Convert 1 m : 25 cm to simplest form.

test.solution: Divide both parts by their HCF, 6.

test.prompt: Five pens cost ₹65. What do eight pens cost?
test.solution: One pen costs 65÷5=13 rupees. Eight pens cost 8×13=104 rupees.

test.prompt: Divide 48 in the ratio 1:3. Find the smaller share.
test.solution: There are 1+3=4 equal parts. One part is 48÷4=12; the smaller share is one part.

test.prompt: At a constant speed, 3 hours cover 180 km. How many kilometres are covered in 5 hours?
test.solution: The speed is 180÷3=60 km per hour. In 5 hours the distance is 60×5=300 km.

test.prompt: Eight equally productive workers take 6 days for a job. How many days would 12 workers take under the same conditions?
test.solution: The job needs 8×6=48 worker-days. Divide by 12 workers: 48÷12=4 days.

concepts.title: Percent means per hundred
concepts.explain: A percentage is a fraction out of 100. To find a percent of a quantity, multiply the quantity by that percentage divided by 100.
steps: 18 correct answers out of 24 give 18/24×100 = 75%.

practice.prompt: Find 30% of 90.
What percentage is 7 out of 20?

concepts.remember: Identify the whole: percentages compare with a base amount.
teaching: Percent means per hundred: 35% = 35/100 = 0.35. To find a percentage of an amount, multiply that amount by the percentage fraction.

For 20% of 250, calculate 20/100 × 250 = 50. Alternatively find 10%, which is 25, and double it. To express a part as a percentage, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. Thus 20 out of 50 is 40%.

concepts.title: Discount, profit and simple interest
concepts.explain: Discount is calculated on marked price; profit percent is usually calculated on cost price. Simple interest uses the original principal throughout.
steps: A 20% discount on ₹500 is ₹100, so pay ₹400.
Cost ₹200, selling price ₹250: profit ₹50; profit percent = 50/200×100 = 25%.

$I=\dfrac{P\times R\times T}{100}$, where $P$ is the principal, $R$ is the annual percentage rate and $T$ is the time in years. For ₹1,500 at $6\%$ for $2$ years: $I=\dfrac{1500\times6\times2}{100}=180$. Interest is ₹180 and the total amount is ₹1,680.

practice.prompt: A ₹800 item has a 10% discount. What is the selling price?
Find simple interest on ₹2,000 at 5% per year for 3 years.

concepts.remember: An increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% does not return to the starting value.
teaching: Identify the base amount before calculating. Discount is usually a percentage of marked price, while profit or loss is a percentage of cost price. Calculate the change, then add or subtract it as required.

A 15% discount on 800 rupees is 120 rupees, leaving 680 rupees to pay. Simple interest uses the same principal each year: $I=\dfrac{PRT}{100}$ when rate is percent per year and time is years. Convert months to years, and add interest to principal only when the total amount is asked.

test.prompt: Cost ₹400, sale ₹460. What is profit percent?
Find interest on ₹3,000 at 4% for 2 years.
A ₹600 bag is discounted 25%. Find its new price.

test.solution: 35/100×80=28. Alternatively, 30% is 24 and 5% is 4; add to get 28.

test.prompt: A pupil answers 27 out of 30 questions correctly. What percentage is correct?
test.solution: 27/30×100=90%. Enter the percentage number 90.

test.prompt: An item costs ₹350 and sells for ₹420. What is the profit in rupees?
test.solution: Profit is selling price minus cost price: 420−350=70.

test.prompt: A ₹800 item has a 15% discount. Find the amount to pay.
Find simple interest on ₹2,000 at 5% per year for 3 years.
test.solution: $I=\dfrac{PRT}{100}=\dfrac{2000\times5\times3}{100}=300$ rupees.

concepts.title: Repeated multiplication
concepts.explain: A power records repeated multiplication. The base is the repeated factor and the exponent counts how many factors.
steps: For the same nonzero base: aᵐ×aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ÷aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
a⁰=1 for a≠0; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ.

practice.prompt: Find 2⁵.
Find 7⁰.
practice.solution: Any nonzero number to power 0 is 1.

concepts.remember: 3² means 3×3, not 3×2.
teaching: A power represents repeated multiplication: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The base is the repeated factor and the exponent counts the factors. It does not mean 2 × 4.

With the same base, multiplying joins factors: 2³ × 2² = 2⁵. Dividing cancels factors: 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³. These rules require the same base, and division requires a nonzero base. They do not apply to addition: 2² + 2³ = 12.

concepts.title: Square and cube roots
concepts.explain: A square root reverses squaring; a cube root reverses cubing. The symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$ means the non-negative square root.

visual.caption: A 3 by 3 by 3 cube contains 27 unit cubes.

steps: √49 = 7 because 7²=49.
∛27 = 3 because 3³=27.
Although x²=49 has solutions ±7, √49 itself is 7.

practice.prompt: Find √121.
Find ∛64.

concepts.remember: In general √(a+b) is not √a+√b.
teaching: A square of side 7 has area 49 square units. A square root reverses squaring, so √49 = 7. The root symbol names the nonnegative square root, although both 7 and −7 square to 49.
A cube root reverses cubing: ∛125 = 5 because 5³ = 125. Locate unfamiliar roots between known squares: 36 < 40 < 49 gives 6 < √40 < 7. Roots need not be whole numbers.

test.solution: A cube means multiplying three copies of the base: 4×4×4=64.
The square root is the nonnegative number whose square is the original number: 12²=144.
The cube root is the number whose cube is the original number: 5³=125.
For equal bases, add exponents when multiplying: 2³ × 2² = 2⁵. Then 2⁵=32.
15×15=225, so the non-negative square root is 15.
6×6×6=216, so the cube root is 6.
For the same nonzero base, subtract exponents: 3⁴÷3²=3²=9.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 2⁻³=1/(2³)=1/8.

concepts.title: Letters stand for numbers
concepts.explain: A variable represents a number that may be unknown or may vary. A term includes its sign. A coefficient multiplies the variable.

visual.caption: 3x + 2: three identical x-boxes and two units

steps: In 3x+2, 3 is the coefficient of x and 2 is the constant term.
If a ticket costs ₹p, five tickets cost ₹5p.

practice.prompt: Find 4x−3 when x=5.
What is the coefficient of y in −6y+9?
practice.solution: The sign belongs to the term: coefficient −6.

concepts.remember: A variable is a number, not a label for an object. 3x means 3×x.
teaching: A letter can represent an unknown or changing number. In 3x + 5, the term 3x means 3 × x, its coefficient is 3 and the constant is 5. When x = 4, substitution gives 3 × 4 + 5 = 17.

An expression describes a value; an equation states that two values are equal. Label what a letter means, including its unit. If x is the price of one pencil, 3x is the price of three; adding 5 might represent a fixed extra charge.

concepts.title: Like terms and brackets
concepts.explain: Like terms have the same variable part, including powers. Combine their coefficients. Multiply every term inside a bracket when expanding.
steps: 3a×2a=6a², while 3a+2a=5a.

practice.prompt: Simplify 7x−2x.
Find 3(x+4) when x=2.

concepts.remember: x and x² are not like terms. Addition and multiplication follow different rules.
teaching: Like terms have the same letter part and powers. Three lots of x plus five lots give 3x + 5x = 8x. But x and x² are different kinds of terms and cannot be combined in this way.

A factor outside brackets multiplies every term: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. A minus sign must also reach every term: −2(x − 3) = −2x + 6. Expand, collect like terms, then check by substituting a small value into both forms.

test.solution: Substitute a = 6: 2a + 7 = 2 × 6 + 7. Therefore 12+7=19.
The coefficient includes the minus sign.
The letter parts match, so add their coefficients: 3+5=8.
Multiply both terms by 2.
The coefficient is the number multiplying y, which is 6.
Like terms share the same variable part. Subtract the coefficients: 7−2=5.
Multiply both terms inside the bracket by 3: 3×x−3×2.
Square first: (−4)²=16. Then multiply by 2: 2×16=32.

concepts.title: Keep both sides balanced
concepts.explain: An equation states that two expressions have the same value. Do the same operation to both sides to keep equality true.

visual.caption: Remove 5 from both sides: x = 7

steps: For 4x=28, divide both sides by 4: x=7.
Substitute back to check the original equation.

practice.prompt: Solve x+9=23.
Solve 6x=54.

concepts.remember: An expression has no equals sign; an equation does.
teaching: An equation is like a balanced scale. Performing the same operation on both sides keeps it balanced. Undo addition with subtraction and multiplication with division by a nonzero number.
For 3x + 4 = 25, subtract 4 from both sides to get 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7. Check: 3 × 7 + 4 = 25. “Moving a term” is shorthand for these equal operations.

concepts.title: Build an equation from a story
concepts.explain: Name the unknown and describe the relationship before calculating. Keep units in your final answer.

visual.caption: Three equal notebook prices plus a ₹4 cover cost ₹25.

steps: Let one notebook cost ₹x. Then 3x+4=25.
Subtract 4: 3x=21. Divide by 3: x=7.
Each notebook costs ₹7. Check: 3×7+4=25.

practice.prompt: Solve 5x−6=29.
A number doubled and increased by 9 is 31. Find the number.

concepts.remember: Do not guess the operation from one word. Write the complete relationship.
teaching: Read a story once for the situation and again for the quantities. Choose a letter for the unknown, then translate each statement. Three identical tickets plus a 4-rupee fee costing 25 rupees gives 3x + 4 = 25.
After solving, return to the story: x = 7 means each ticket costs 7 rupees. Substitute into the total and include the unit. A negative count of objects is a reason to revisit the model or arithmetic.

test.solution: Add 8 to both sides.
Divide by 7.
Multiply both sides by 4.

test.prompt: Four tickets and a ₹10 fee cost ₹110. Find one ticket’s price.

test.solution: Subtract 19 from both sides: x=42−19=23.
Add 5 to both sides: 6x=36. Divide by 6: x=6.
Divide both sides by 2: x+3=11. Subtract 3: x=8.
Subtract 2: x/5=7. Multiply by 5: x=35.

test.prompt: Three identical notebooks and a ₹12 pen cost ₹87. Find one notebook price.
test.solution: Let a notebook cost x rupees. 3x+12=87, so 3x=75 and x=25.

concepts.title: Measure a turn
concepts.explain: An angle measures the turn between two rays with the same endpoint. A right angle is 90°, a straight angle 180°, and a full turn 360°.

visual.caption: 60° is an acute angle: smaller than a right angle.

steps: Acute: between 0° and 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°.
Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°.
An angle of 35° has complement 55°.

practice.prompt: Find the supplement of 125°.
What type of angle is 110°?

concepts.remember: Longer rays do not make an angle larger; the turn determines the angle.
teaching: An angle measures a turn between two rays meeting at a vertex. A quarter-turn is 90°, a half-turn is 180° and a complete turn is 360°. Making the rays longer does not change the angle.

Centre a protractor at the vertex and align its baseline with one ray. Use the scale starting at zero on that ray. Complementary angles total 90°; supplementary angles total 180°. Subtract the known part from the appropriate total.

concepts.title: Intersecting and parallel lines
concepts.explain: Opposite angles at an intersection are equal. Adjacent angles on a straight line add to 180°. When parallel lines meet a transversal, corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal.
steps: If one angle at an intersection is 65°, its opposite is 65°.
Its adjacent angle is 180−65=115°.
Corresponding angles are equal only when the two lines are parallel.

practice.prompt: An angle and its adjacent angle form a straight line. One is 72°. Find the other.
One angle at an intersection is 47°. Find its vertically opposite angle.

concepts.remember: A diagram is not proof of parallel lines; look for stated conditions or matching marks.
teaching: Opposite angles at an intersection are vertically opposite and equal. Adjacent angles on a straight line add to 180°. Use these facts to work around an intersection one angle at a time.

When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal. Interior angles on the same side total 180°. Confirm that the lines are parallel; their appearance alone is not enough. State the relationship before calculating.

test.prompt: How many degrees in a full turn?
test.solution: One complete rotation is 360°.
Complementary angles add to 90°. Subtract the given angle: 90−28=62°.

test.prompt: An angle is 84°. Find its vertically opposite angle.
test.solution: Opposite angles are equal.

test.prompt: Corresponding angles on parallel lines: one is 118°. Find the other.
test.solution: Corresponding angles are equal.

test.prompt: How many degrees are in three right angles?
test.solution: A right angle is 90°. Three give 3×90=270°.

test.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are 47° and x°. Find x.
test.solution: A straight angle is 180°. Subtract: 180−47=133°.

test.prompt: Around a point, three angles are 90°, 120° and x°. Find x.
test.solution: Angles around a point total 360°. Thus x=360−90−120=150°.
125° is greater than 90° and less than 180°.

test.prompt: Alternate interior angles on parallel lines: one is 73°. Find the other.
test.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal when the lines are parallel.

concepts.title: Triangle facts
concepts.explain: A triangle has three sides. Its interior angles total 180°. The sum of any two side lengths must be greater than the third.
steps: Equilateral: 3 equal sides and 3 angles of 60°.
Isosceles: at least 2 equal sides; angles opposite them are equal.
If two angles are 45° and 65°, the third is 180−45−65=70°.

practice.prompt: Two triangle angles are 35° and 85°. Find the third.
Can 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm form a triangle?

concepts.remember: A triangle inequality is strict. Lengths 2, 3 and 5 form a straight segment, not a triangle.
teaching: A triangle has three sides, and its interior angles total 180°. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and equal opposite angles. An equilateral triangle has all three angles equal to 60°.

The sum of any two side lengths must be greater than the third. Sides 3, 4 and 8 cannot form a triangle because 3 + 4 is too short to meet across a side of 8. Check this before using proposed triangle measurements.

concepts.title: Four-sided shapes
concepts.explain: A quadrilateral’s interior angles total 360°. A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel. Rectangles, rhombi and squares are special parallelograms.

visual.caption: Rectangle: four right angles and equal opposite sides

steps: A rectangle has four right angles. A rhombus has four equal sides.
A square has both properties. Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
Three quadrilateral angles are 80°, 95°, 105°; the fourth is 360−280=80°.

practice.prompt: Three quadrilateral angles are 90°, 70° and 120°. Find the fourth.
Is every square a rectangle?
practice.solution: A square meets the definition of rectangle.

concepts.remember: Classify using properties, not the orientation or appearance of the drawing.
teaching: A diagonal divides a quadrilateral into two triangles, so its interior angles total 360°. Side and angle properties distinguish parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses and squares.

A rectangle has four right angles; a rhombus has four equal sides. A square has both properties, so it is also a rectangle and a rhombus. A parallelogram has equal opposite sides and angles; do not assume all four are equal.

test.prompt: An equilateral triangle has each angle equal to how many degrees?
test.solution: The three equal angles of an equilateral triangle total 180°. Divide equally: 180÷3=60°.

test.prompt: Triangle angles 40° and 75°: find the third.
What is the sum of quadrilateral angles?
test.solution: A diagonal divides it into two triangles.

test.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle 110°. Find an adjacent angle.
test.solution: Adjacent angles sum to 180°.

test.prompt: Can 4, 5 and 8 be triangle side lengths?
test.solution: All three pair sums exceed the remaining side.

test.prompt: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. Find each equal base angle.
test.solution: The other two angles total 180−40=140°. They are equal, so each is 140÷2=70°.

test.prompt: A triangle has angles 90° and 35°. Find the third angle.
test.solution: Subtract known angles from 180°: 180−90−35=55°.

test.prompt: Can 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm be sides of a triangle?
test.solution: The sum 2+3=5 is less than 6, so the sides cannot close to form a triangle.

test.prompt: Three quadrilateral angles are 90°, 85° and 95°. Find the fourth.
test.solution: The total is 360°. Known angles sum to 270°, leaving 90°.

test.prompt: A parallelogram has one angle 68°. Find its opposite angle.
test.solution: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

concepts.title: Reflections and rotations
concepts.explain: A line of symmetry divides a shape into matching mirror halves. Rotational symmetry means a shape fits itself before completing a full turn.

visual.caption: The dashed line divides this shape into matching halves.

steps: A non-square rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry and rotational order 2.
A square has 4 lines and rotational order 4.
Rotational order 4 means a match every 360÷4=90°.

practice.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
practice.solution: Two diagonals and two lines through opposite side midpoints.

practice.prompt: A shape matches every 120° turn. What is its rotational order?

concepts.remember: A diagonal of a non-square rectangle is not a line of symmetry.
teaching: A line of symmetry divides a figure into halves that match exactly when folded. Matching points lie at the same perpendicular distance on opposite sides of the fold. A figure can have no symmetry lines, one or several.

Rotational symmetry means a figure matches itself after a turn smaller than 360°. A nonsquare rectangle matches after 180°, giving order 2. A square matches every 90°, giving order 4. Reflection and rotation are different movements; test each separately.

concepts.title: Construct and read scale drawings
concepts.explain: Use a ruler for lengths and a protractor for angles. A perpendicular bisector passes through a segment’s midpoint at 90°. A scale relates drawing distance to actual distance.

visual.caption: Equal compass arcs above and below AB locate its perpendicular bisector.

steps: Open a compass to more than half AB. Draw equal-radius arcs from A and B.
Join the two arc intersections. The joining line bisects AB at 90°.
At scale 1 cm:2 m, a 5 cm line represents 10 m.

practice.prompt: A segment is 14 cm long. How far is its midpoint from an endpoint?
At scale 1 cm:3 m, what actual distance does 4 cm represent?

concepts.remember: A perpendicular line need not bisect a segment. A perpendicular bisector must do both.
teaching: Construct from the given measurements rather than copying the appearance of a sketch. Draw and label a starting side, then locate the other points with a ruler, compass or protractor. Keep construction marks that explain your method.

A scale drawing keeps length ratios constant. If 1 cm represents 2 m, a 5 cm line represents 10 m. Convert units before comparing. Doubling both dimensions makes the area four times as large, so a length scale factor cannot be applied directly to area.

test.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
test.solution: One from each vertex to the opposite midpoint.

test.prompt: What is the rotational order of a square?
test.solution: It matches at each 90° turn.

test.prompt: Half of a 17 cm segment is how many cm?
test.solution: A midpoint divides a segment into two equal lengths: 17÷2=8.5.

test.prompt: Scale 1 cm:5 m. A 6 cm drawing represents how many metres?
test.solution: Each centimetre on the drawing represents 5 metres, so multiply by six: 6×5=30.

test.prompt: At what angle does a perpendicular bisector cross its segment?
test.solution: Perpendicular means 90°.

test.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a non-square rectangle have?
test.solution: One line passes through the midpoints of the long sides and one through the short sides. Diagonals are not symmetry lines.

test.prompt: A shape has rotational order 6. Find its smallest positive matching turn in degrees.
test.solution: Divide a full turn by the order: 360÷6=60°.

test.prompt: A map scale is 1 cm:4 km. How many kilometres does 7 cm represent?
test.solution: Each centimetre represents 4 km, so 7×4=28 km.

test.prompt: A drawing scale is 1 cm:3 m. How many centimetres represent 24 m?
test.solution: Divide the actual distance by metres per centimetre: 24÷3=8 cm.

test.prompt: A perpendicular bisector meets a 26 cm segment at its midpoint. Find either half-length in cm.
test.solution: A midpoint divides a segment equally: 26÷2=13 cm.

concepts.title: Boundary and surface
concepts.explain: Perimeter measures distance around a boundary. Area measures how much surface is covered. Count unit squares to understand area before using formulas.

visual.caption: 7 columns × 4 rows = 28 square units; perimeter = 22 units.

steps: $P=2(l+b)$, where $l$ is the length and $b$ is the breadth. For $l=7\text{ cm}$ and $b=4\text{ cm}$: $P=2(7+4)=22\text{ cm}$.
$A=l\times b=7\times4=28\text{ cm}^2$.
A square of side s has perimeter 4s and area s².

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a 9 cm by 5 cm rectangle.
Find the area of a square with side 6 cm.

concepts.remember: Perimeter uses units such as cm; area uses square units such as cm².
teaching: Perimeter is the distance around a boundary, measured in length units. Area is the surface inside, measured in square units. A fence needs perimeter; floor covering needs area.

For a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm, perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm. Area is 8 × 5 = 40 square centimetres because there are five rows of eight unit squares. In a compound shape, distinguish outer edges from internal dividing lines.

concepts.title: Triangles, parallelograms and trapeziums
concepts.explain: Use the perpendicular height, not the sloping side. A triangle occupies half of a matching parallelogram. Split composite figures into familiar pieces.

visual.caption: Triangle area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm²

steps: $A=\dfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.
$A=\text{base}\times\text{height}$.

$A=\dfrac12(a+b)h$, where $a$ and $b$ are the parallel sides and $h$ is the perpendicular height. For sides $8\text{ cm}$ and $14\text{ cm}$ and height $5\text{ cm}$: $A=\dfrac12(8+14)\times5=55\text{ cm}^2$.

practice.prompt: Find a triangle’s area with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm.
A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 4 cm. Find its area.

concepts.remember: Draw the height perpendicular to the base; it may lie outside an obtuse triangle.
teaching: A parallelogram rearranges into a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height, so its area is base times height. A triangle is half a matching parallelogram, giving half the base times perpendicular height.

Height must meet the base at a right angle; a sloping side is usually not height. A trapezium has area half the sum of its parallel sides times their perpendicular separation. Mark these lengths on the picture before substituting into a formula.

test.prompt: Perimeter of a square of side 11 cm?
test.solution: A square has four equal sides. Add all four, or multiply one side by four: 4×11=44.

test.prompt: Area of a 13 cm by 4 cm rectangle?
test.solution: Multiply length by breadth to count the unit squares: 13×4=52.

test.prompt: Triangle base 8 cm, height 9 cm: area?
test.solution: A triangle has half the area of a parallelogram with the same base and perpendicular height: ½×8×9=36.

test.prompt: Trapezium parallel sides 6 and 10 cm, height 4 cm: area?
test.solution: Add the parallel sides, multiply by perpendicular height and halve: ½×16×4=32.

test.prompt: A 6 m by 5 m floor uses 1 m² tiles. How many tiles, ignoring gaps?
test.solution: Area 30 m²; each tile covers 1 m².

test.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide.
test.solution: Add all four sides: 9+6+9+6=30 cm, or use 2(9+6).

test.prompt: Find the area of a square of side 12 cm.
test.solution: Area=side×side=12×12=144 cm².

test.prompt: A parallelogram has base 11 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area.
test.solution: Area=base×height=11×5=55 cm².

test.prompt: A triangle has area 48 cm² and base 12 cm. Find its perpendicular height.
A rectangular garden 14 m by 8 m needs fencing with a 2 m gate left open. How many metres of fencing are needed?
test.solution: Perimeter=2(14+8)=44 m. Leave 2 m for the gate: 44−2=42 m.

concepts.title: Faces, edges and nets
concepts.explain: A solid occupies space. Flat surfaces are faces; faces meet along edges, and edges meet at vertices. A net unfolds a solid’s surface onto a plane.

visual.caption: Cube: 6 square faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices

steps: A cuboid has 6 rectangular faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
A cube has six equal square faces.
A cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface.

practice.prompt: How many vertices does a cuboid have?
practice.solution: There are four on the top and four on the bottom.

practice.prompt: How many square faces does a cube have?
practice.solution: Top, bottom, front, back, left and right.

concepts.remember: A curved surface is not a polygonal face. Use the description stated in a question.
teaching: A solid is three-dimensional. Flat surfaces are faces, edges are where faces meet, and vertices are corners. A net lays surfaces flat to show how they fold together.

A cube has six square faces, twelve edges and eight vertices. A cuboid also has six faces, but they need not all be squares. Remember hidden edges. Curved solids need different descriptions: a cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface.

concepts.title: Measure capacity and covering
concepts.explain: Volume counts unit cubes filling a solid. Surface area counts square units covering it. Capacity is often measured in litres.

visual.caption: A cube of side 5 cm has volume 125 cm³ and total surface area 150 cm².

steps: $V=l\times b\times h=8\times3\times2=48\text{ cm}^3$.
Cuboid total surface area = 2(lb+bh+hl).
Cube volume = s³; total surface area = 6s².
1 litre = 1,000 cm³; 1 mL = 1 cm³.

practice.prompt: Volume of a 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm cuboid?
How many litres are 2,500 cm³?

concepts.remember: Area measures covering; volume measures filling. Do not interchange cm² and cm³.
teaching: Volume counts unit cubes inside. A cuboid has length times breadth cubes in each layer and height layers, giving length × breadth × height. Surface area measures the outside covering instead.

A box 5 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm has volume 60 cubic centimetres. Its total surface area is twice the sum of its three different face areas. Use consistent units. Capacity measures what a container holds: 1 cubic centimetre equals 1 millilitre; 1,000 millilitres equals 1 litre.

test.prompt: How many edges has a cube?
test.solution: Four top, four bottom, four vertical.

test.prompt: Volume of a cube of side 4 cm?
test.solution: A cube contains side × side × side unit cubes: 4³=64.

test.prompt: Total surface area of a cube of side 3 cm?
test.solution: There are six square faces, each of area 3² square centimetres: 6×3²=54.

test.prompt: How many cm³ are in 3 litres?
Volume of a 10 cm by 5 cm by 2 cm box?
How many vertices does a cuboid have?
test.solution: A cuboid has four vertices on its top face and four on its bottom face, giving 8.

test.prompt: Find the volume of a cuboid 7 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm.
test.solution: Volume=length×breadth×height=7×4×3=84 cm³.

test.prompt: Find the total surface area of a cube of side 5 cm.
test.solution: Each square face has area 25 cm². Six faces give 6×25=150 cm².

test.prompt: How many litres are equal to 4,500 cm³?
test.solution: 1 litre=1,000 cm³. Divide 4,500 by 1,000 to get 4.5 litres.

test.prompt: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm.

concepts.title: Read, organise and summarise data
concepts.explain: A frequency is how often a value occurs. Read the labels and scale before interpreting a graph. Mean shares the total equally; median is the middle ordered value; mode is most frequent.
steps: Tuesday has 7 books borrowed, the largest of these three counts.
Range = largest−smallest = 6−2=4.

practice.prompt: Find the mean of 3, 7 and 8.
Find the median of 9, 2, 5.

concepts.remember: For an even number of data values, median is the mean of the two middle values.
teaching: Organise observations before calculating. The mean shares the total equally, the median is the middle value after sorting, and the mode is the most frequent value. The range is largest minus smallest.
For 2, 3, 3, 8, the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The median is the average of the two middle values, 3; the mode is 3; the range is 6. An unusual large value can move the mean without changing the median.

concepts.title: Probability of equally likely outcomes
concepts.explain: Probability measures chance from 0 to 1. For a finite set of equally likely outcomes, divide favourable outcomes by total possible outcomes.
steps: From 3 red and 2 blue equally sized counters mixed in a bag, P(red)=3/5.
For a fair die, P(even)=3/6=1/2.
Impossible events have probability 0; certain events have probability 1.

practice.prompt: A fair die has how many possible outcomes?
What is the probability of heads on a fair coin?
practice.solution: One favourable outcome out of two equally likely outcomes.

concepts.remember: Counting outcomes this way needs equal likelihood; do not assume all real-world events are equally likely.
teaching: List possible outcomes before finding probability. For equally likely outcomes, divide the number of favourable outcomes by the total. An impossible event has probability 0; a certain event has probability 1.

A fair die has six outcomes, three of them even, so the probability of an even result is 3/6 = 1/2. Equal likelihood matters: simple outcome counting is not enough for an unfair die. Probability describes a long-run tendency, not a promise about the next throw.

test.solution: Add the observations: 5 + 9 + 10 = 24. Divide by the three observations: 24÷3=8.
3 occurs most often.
Range is the largest value minus the smallest: 15−6=9.

test.prompt: Probability of a number greater than 4 on a fair die?

test.solution: Add to get 36 and divide by the four values: 36÷4=9.
Order the values: 2,4,6,7,9. The third value, 6, is in the middle.
The maximum is 18 and the minimum is 5. Range=18−5=13.

test.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue identical balls. Find the probability of choosing red.
test.solution: There are 4 favourable outcomes among 10 equally likely balls: 4/10=2/5.

test.prompt: What is the probability of rolling a 7 on a standard six-sided die?
test.solution: The possible results are 1 through 6. Rolling 7 is impossible, so its probability is 0.

concepts.title: Fractions can be negative too
concepts.explain: A rational number can be written p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. Integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are rational numbers.

visual.caption: The magnitude of −3/4 is three quarters. The minus sign places it left of zero.

steps: −1/4 is greater than −3/4 because it is closer to zero.
A rational number has infinitely many equivalent forms: −3/4 = −6/8.

practice.prompt: Which is greater?
practice.solution: On a number line −1/4 is to the right of −3/4.

practice.prompt: Write −0.5 as a fraction.

concepts.remember: Zero is rational: 0 = 0/1. A denominator can never be zero.
teaching: A rational number is an integer divided by a nonzero integer. A negative sign can be in front of the fraction or on exactly one of its parts: −3/4 = 3/(−4) = −0.75. Two negative parts give a positive fraction.

Compare negative fractions on a number line. Since −1/4 is farther right than −3/4, it is greater. Multiply both parts by the same nonzero number to make equivalent forms: −3/4 = −6/8. A denominator can never be zero.

concepts.title: Calculate with signed fractions
concepts.explain: Use common denominators for addition and subtraction. Multiply fractions using the sign rules. To divide by a nonzero fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
concepts.remember: Subtraction of a negative adds the positive opposite.
teaching: Use a positive common denominator for addition, then add the signed numerators. For −2/3 + 5/6, first write −2/3 = −4/6. Then −4/6 + 5/6 = 1/6.

Apply integer sign rules when multiplying fractions: (−2/3) × (−3/4) = 6/12 = 1/2. For division, multiply by the reciprocal of the nonzero divisor. Brackets around negative factors make the signs easier to follow.

test.solution: It can be expressed as an integer over a nonzero integer: −7 = −7/1.
Add signed numerators.
Two negatives give a positive.
Use denominator 8: −5/8+2/8=−3/8.
The signs differ, so the product is negative. Simplify −42/63 to −2/3.
Multiply by the reciprocal: (−5/6)×(−12/5)=60/30=2.
These are opposite numbers, so their sum is zero.

concepts.title: Rational or irrational?
concepts.explain: Rational numbers have terminating or recurring decimal forms. An irrational number has a non-terminating decimal with no repeating block. Both belong to the real numbers.
steps: A root of a perfect square is an integer, such as √81 = 9.
0.121212… repeats the block 12, so it is rational.

practice.prompt: Simplify √72.
Which is irrational?

concepts.remember: A long decimal display alone does not prove that a number is irrational.
teaching: Rational numbers have terminating or eventually repeating decimals. Irrational numbers have decimals that never terminate or settle into a repeating pattern. Together they form the real numbers on the number line.

Not every root is irrational: √49 = 7 is rational, but √2 is irrational. Since 1.4² = 1.96 and 1.5² = 2.25, √2 lies between 1.4 and 1.5. A rounded decimal approximates the irrational value; it does not equal it exactly.

concepts.title: Root operations and rationalising
concepts.explain: For non-negative a and b, √a × √b = √(ab). Combine only like root terms. Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero expression when rationalising.
steps: (a+b)(a−b)=a²−b² helps with two-term denominators.

practice.prompt: Find √8 × √2.
Simplify 2√5 + 3√5.
practice.solution: Add the coefficients of the same root.

concepts.remember: √(a+b) is generally not √a + √b.
teaching: Separate a perfect-square factor to simplify a root: √45 = √(9 × 5) = 3√5. Like roots combine as like terms: 2√5 + 3√5 = 5√5. Unlike roots cannot normally be collected into one term.

For 2/√5, multiply numerator and denominator by √5 to get 2√5/5. This works because √5 × √5 = 5 and the multiplying fraction equals 1. Square roots do not distribute over addition; for example, √(9 + 16) = 5, whereas √9 + √16 = 7.

test.solution: The required square root is nonnegative. Check its square: 14² = 196.
Separate the perfect square: √45 = √(9 × 5) = 3√5, because 45 = 9×5.
Combine the nonnegative roots: √6 × √24 = √(6 × 24). Therefore √144 = 12.
The digits repeat in a fixed block.
Multiply top and bottom by √7.
Multiply inside the root: √(5×20)=√100=10.
The root parts match, so subtract coefficients: (8−5)√3=3√3.
√64=8, which is an integer and therefore rational.
Multiply numerator and denominator by √5: 2√5/5.

concepts.title: See an identity as an area
concepts.explain: An identity is an equation that is true for every value of its variables. The square of a sum means multiplying the whole sum by itself. In the picture, the square of side a + b contains one a² region, two ab regions and one b² region. Together their areas give a² + 2ab + b².

visual.caption: The square of side a+b splits into a², ab, ab and b².

practice.prompt: Coefficient of x in (x+6)²?
practice.solution: Use $(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$ with $a=x$ and $b=6$. $$\begin{aligned}(x+6)^2&=x^2+2\times x\times6+6^2\\&=x^2+12x+36\end{aligned}$$ The coefficient of $x$ is the number multiplying $x$. In $12x$, that number is $12$.

practice.prompt: Find 49² using (50−1)².
practice.solution: Write $49=50-1$, so $49^2=(50-1)^2$. Use $(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$ with $a=50$ and $b=1$. $$\begin{aligned}49^2&=50^2-2\times50\times1+1^2\\&=2500-100+1\\&=2400+1\\&=2401\end{aligned}$$ Here $50^2=2500$, twice the product is $2\times50\times1=100$, and $1^2=1$. The last term is added. Remember: $49^2$ means $49\times49$.

concepts.remember: The middle term 2ab is essential in a square of a sum.

workedExamples.title: Square of a sum
workedExamples.meaning: Square the first term, add twice the product of the two terms, then add the square of the second term. The two rectangles in the picture give ab + ab = 2ab.
workedExamples.conclusion: The middle term is $2\times x\times4=8x$. Squaring a sum does not mean squaring each term alone.

workedExamples.title: Square of a difference
workedExamples.meaning: Square the first term, subtract twice the product, then add the square of the second term. The final term is positive because a negative multiplied by a negative is positive.
workedExamples.conclusion: The middle term is $-8x$, but the last term is $+16$.

workedExamples.title: Product of a sum and a difference
workedExamples.meaning: The two brackets have the same terms, with opposite signs between them. When expanded, the middle terms cancel.
workedExamples.conclusion: Using the identity directly: $x^2-4^2=x^2-16$. There is no middle term because $-4x+4x=0$.

teaching: An identity is true for every allowed value of its letters. Expand (a + b)² as (a + b)(a + b). Multiplying every term gives a² + ab + ab + b². The two middle rectangles combine to make 2ab.

For (x + 4)², identify a = x and b = 4. The middle term is 2 × x × 4 = 8x and the final square is 16. With subtraction, the middle term becomes negative but the final square stays positive. Follow each substitution in the examples below.

concepts.title: Factorise by reversing multiplication
concepts.explain: First remove a common factor if one exists. Then look for an identity or a pair of numbers whose sum and product match a quadratic expression.

practice.prompt: Factorise x²−36.
practice.solution: Use the difference of two squares.

practice.prompt: Find the positive missing number: x²+9x+20=(x+4)(x+□).

concepts.remember: Check a factorisation by expanding it again.
teaching: Factorisation reverses expansion by writing a sum or difference as a product. First look for a common factor: 6x + 12 = 6(x + 2). Multiplying the brackets back checks the result.
For x² + 8x + 16, the outside terms are x² and 4², and the middle is 2 × x × 4, so it is (x + 4)². For x² − 16, the difference of squares gives (x + 4)(x − 4). Check both signs and the middle term.

test.solution: In (x + 7)² = x² + 14x + 49, the constant is the square of 7: 7² = 49.
Take out the common factor 5x.

test.prompt: Find the coefficient of x in (x+9)².
test.solution: Using (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b² gives x²+18x+81, so the coefficient is 18.
The expansion is x²−16x+64. The constant term is (−8)²=64.
Use a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b) with a=x and b=9.
The numbers must add to 11 and multiply to 24. Since 3+8=11 and 3×8=24, k=8.

concepts.title: An ordered pair fixes a point
concepts.explain: The first coordinate is horizontal distance from the origin; the second is vertical distance. Signs specify direction. The order matters.

visual.caption: P(3,2): move 3 right, then 2 up.

steps: (3,2) and (2,3) are different points.
(−2,4) is left of the y-axis and above the x-axis.
Points on the x-axis have y=0. Points on the y-axis have x=0.

practice.prompt: What is the y-coordinate of (−5,7)?
A point on the y-axis has x equal to what?

concepts.remember: The axes meet at (0,0), the origin.
teaching: The horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis meet at the origin, (0, 0). An ordered pair gives the horizontal coordinate first and vertical coordinate second. Changing their order usually changes the point.
To plot (−3, 2), move three units left and two up from the origin. Negative x means left; negative y means down. Points on the y-axis have x = 0; points on the x-axis have y = 0.
