concepts.title: A linear equation has many solutions
concepts.explain: A pair (x,y) solves an equation if substituting both values makes it true. A linear equation in two variables represents a straight line.

visual.caption: The line y=2x+1 passes through (0,1), (1,3) and (2,5).

steps: For y=2x+1: x=0 gives y=1; x=1 gives y=3; x=2 gives y=5.
Plot these points and join them with a straight line.
For x+y=7, (2,5) is one of infinitely many solutions.

practice.prompt: For y=3x−2, find y when x=4.
Does (3,4) satisfy x+y=7?

concepts.remember: One equation in two variables usually does not determine one unique pair.
teaching: An equation in two variables can have many solution pairs. For x + y = 5, choosing x = 1 gives y = 4, while x = 2 gives y = 3. Both satisfy the condition.

Make a table, check each pair in the equation, then plot on axes with a consistent scale. Draw the line through the points. Points on the line are solutions; points off it fail the equation. One equation usually does not determine a unique pair.

test.solution: The first coordinate is x.

test.prompt: y-coordinate of a point on the x-axis?
test.solution: All points on the x-axis have y=0.

test.prompt: For y=4x+3, find y at x=2.
test.solution: Substitute x = 2: y = 4 × 2 + 3. Hence 8+3 = 11.

test.prompt: For x+y=9 and x=5, find y.
test.solution: Subtract x = 5 from both sides of x + y = 9: 9−5=4.

test.prompt: Which point lies in the third quadrant?
test.solution: Both coordinates are negative.

test.prompt: What is the x-coordinate of a point on the y-axis?
test.solution: Every point on the y-axis has no horizontal displacement, so x=0.
x is positive and y is negative, which describes the fourth quadrant.

test.prompt: For y=5x−4, find y when x=3.
test.solution: Substitute x=3: y=15−4=11.
Substitute: 8+y=12. Subtract 8 to get y=4.
3×2−1=6−1=5, matching the given y-coordinate.

concepts.title: Two conditions, one pair
concepts.explain: A solution must satisfy both equations at the same time. Think of the equations as two clues about the same unknown quantities.
steps: Adding these equations cancels y because +y and −y add to zero.
Substitute x=7 into x+y=11 to get y=4.
Check both clues: 7+4=11 and 7−4=3.

practice.prompt: If x+y=13 and x−y=5, find x.
For the same equations, find y.

concepts.remember: Always check the pair in both original equations.
teaching: Two equations describe two conditions on the same unknowns. A solution must satisfy both. Elimination cancels an unknown by adding or subtracting equations; substitution replaces one unknown with an equivalent expression.

For x + y = 9 and x − y = 3, add to get 2x = 12. Hence x = 6 and substitution gives y = 3. Check both original equations. On a graph, the solution is an intersection; distinct parallel lines have no common solution.

concepts.title: Turn a situation into two equations
concepts.explain: Choose variables with clear meanings and keep the units consistent. One statement gives one equation; the second independent statement gives another.
steps: Let p be the price of a pen and n the price of a notebook.
2p+n=44 and p+n=32. Subtract to get p=12.
Then n=32−12=20. Two pens and one notebook cost 24+20=44.

practice.prompt: A pen and a pad cost ₹35. Two pens and a pad cost ₹47. Find the pen price.
For those prices, find the pad price.

concepts.remember: Parallel distinct lines have no common solution; coincident lines have infinitely many.
teaching: Use two letters when a story has two different unknown quantities. Define them before making equations. A total number of tickets and their total cost give different conditions when adult and child prices differ.
Three adult tickets at x rupees and two child tickets at y rupees cost 3x + 2y, not 5xy. After solving, verify both the count and cost. State what each answer means and include the units.

test.solution: Add: 2x=22.

test.prompt: For x+y=18 and x−y=4, find y.
test.solution: Adding the equations gives 2x = 22, so x = 11. Substitute into x + y = 18: 18−11=7.
Subtract the second equation from the first.

test.prompt: A ticket and a snack cost ₹90; two tickets and a snack cost ₹145. Find one ticket price.
test.solution: The second purchase has exactly one extra ticket and the same snack. Subtract the costs: 145−90=55.

test.prompt: Do x+y=4 and x+y=6 have a common solution?
test.solution: The same sum cannot be both 4 and 6.
Add the equations: 2x=26. Divide by 2: x=13.

test.prompt: For x+y=20 and x−y=6, find y.
test.solution: Substitute x=13 in x+y=20: y=20−13=7.
Subtract the second equation from the first: 2x=12, so x=6.

test.prompt: Two pens and a notebook cost ₹62. One pen and the same notebook cost ₹47. Find the notebook price.
test.solution: Subtract the bills to find one pen: 62−47=15. Notebook price=47−15=32.

test.prompt: How many solutions do x+y=5 and 2x+2y=10 have?
test.solution: The second equation is twice the first, so both describe the same line.

concepts.title: A squared unknown changes the equation
concepts.explain: A quadratic equation has the form ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. If a product is zero, at least one factor is zero. This gives a way to solve a factorised quadratic.
steps: Find numbers whose sum is −5 and product is 6: −2 and −3.
Set each factor equal to zero.

practice.prompt: Which are the roots of x²−7x+12=0?
A square has area 81 cm². Find its side in cm.
practice.solution: s²=81; a length is positive, so s=9.

concepts.remember: An equation may have two roots, but a word problem can rule out a negative length.
teaching: A quadratic equation has highest power 2. Arrange it with zero on one side before factorising. A product is zero only when at least one factor is zero; this lets us solve simpler equations.
For x² − 5x + 6 = 0, choose −2 and −3: their product is 6 and sum is −5. Then (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 gives x = 2 or x = 3. Check each root. Do not divide away a factor that might be zero.

concepts.title: An arithmetic progression adds the same amount
concepts.explain: In an arithmetic progression, the difference between consecutive terms is constant. To reach the nth term from the first term, add the difference n−1 times.
steps: The 10th term is 5+9×4=41.
For 20,17,14,… the difference is −3.
In 2,4,8,16,… the differences change, so this is not an arithmetic progression.

practice.prompt: Find the 6th term of 3,8,13,…
Find the common difference of 24,19,14,…

concepts.remember: Use n−1 steps, not n, when starting from the first term.
teaching: An arithmetic progression has a constant difference between consecutive terms. For 5, 8, 11, 14, the first term is 5 and each jump is 3. There is one jump to the second term and two to the third.

The nth term uses n − 1 jumps: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. The tenth term here is 5 + 9 × 3 = 32. A sequence that repeatedly multiplies is not generally an arithmetic progression. Check consecutive differences first.

test.prompt: Positive root of x²−6x+8=0 that is larger?
test.solution: The roots are 2 and 4.
The first term is 4 and each jump is 3. Reaching term 8 takes seven jumps: 4+7×3=25.
Subtract 4.
The differences are 2,6,18.
Factorise: (x−3)(x−5)=0, so x=3 or x=5.

test.prompt: A square has area 121 cm². Find its side length in cm.
test.solution: s²=121 gives s=±11. A side length is positive, so choose 11 cm.
The difference is 4. Use aₙ=a+(n−1)d: 2+11×4=46.
Subtract a term from the next: 11−17=−6.
The common difference is −3. The fifth term is 25+4×(−3)=13.

concepts.title: Distance makes a right triangle
concepts.explain: Horizontal change is $x_2-x_1$ and vertical change is $y_2-y_1$. The segment joining the points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, so its length is $\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$.

visual.caption: From A(1,1) to B(5,4): 4 units across, 3 units up, 5 units along the segment.

steps: A(1,1), B(5,4): horizontal change=4, vertical change=3.
Distance²=4²+3²=25, so distance=5.
Distance is never negative; swapping the points gives the same result.

practice.prompt: Distance from (0,0) to (6,8)?
Distance from (−2,3) to (4,3)?
practice.solution: The points share y=3, so the horizontal distance is 4−(−2)=6.

concepts.remember: Square the whole coordinate difference, including its sign.
teaching: The horizontal and vertical differences between points form the legs of a right triangle. The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse: square both differences, add and take the square root.

From (1, 2) to (4, 6), differences are 3 and 4, so distance is √(3² + 4²) = 5 units. Subtract in the same order for both coordinates. Adding unsquared differences measures a different path, not the straight-line distance.

concepts.title: Midpoint means halfway in both directions
concepts.explain: Average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates separately. The midpoint is ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
steps: The midpoint of (−2,1) and (6,5) is (2,3).
The midpoint need not have integer coordinates.
For (0,0) and (3,5), the midpoint is (1.5,2.5).

practice.prompt: Find the x-coordinate of the midpoint of (2,3) and (8,7).
Find the y-coordinate of the same midpoint.

concepts.remember: Do not mix an x-coordinate with a y-coordinate in the average.
teaching: A midpoint is halfway along a line segment. Average the x-coordinates for the horizontal halfway position and average the y-coordinates for the vertical halfway position.

For (2, 1) and (8, 5), the midpoint is (5, 3), because (2 + 8)/2 = 5 and (1 + 5)/2 = 3. Negative coordinates work the same way. Each midpoint coordinate should lie between its two endpoint coordinates.

test.solution: Vertical distance=2−(−4)=6.
The midpoint y-coordinate is the average of the endpoint y-coordinates: (2+8)/2=5.

test.prompt: Does swapping the two endpoints change the distance?
test.solution: The squared differences stay the same.
Changes are 3 and 4. Distance=√(3²+4²)=√25=5 units.
The y-coordinates match. Horizontal distance=3−(−5)=8 units.
Average the x-coordinates: (−8+2)/2=−6/2=−3.
Average the y-coordinates: (−3+7)/2=4/2=2.

test.prompt: A segment starts at (0,0) and has midpoint (3,4). Find the other endpoint’s x-coordinate.
test.solution: If the other x-coordinate is x, then (0+x)/2=3. Multiply by 2: x=6.

concepts.title: Same shape, different size
concepts.explain: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. A scale factor multiplies every corresponding length by the same number.

visual.caption: Two right triangles with sides 3,4,5 and 6,8,10. Every length is doubled.

steps: The triangles 3,4,5 and 6,8,10 have scale factor 2.
A length of 7 cm becomes 21 cm under scale factor 3.
Areas scale by the square of the length factor: doubling lengths multiplies area by 4.

practice.prompt: A triangle is enlarged by factor 3. A 5 cm side becomes how many cm?
If lengths are multiplied by 3, areas are multiplied by what?

concepts.remember: Match corresponding sides before forming ratios.
teaching: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Mark matching vertices first. A scale factor of 3 multiplies every corresponding length by 3.

Areas scale by the square of the length factor, so a length factor of 3 gives an area factor of 9. Write side ratios in the same corresponding order, then solve for an unknown length. Appearance alone does not prove similarity.

concepts.title: Name sides from the chosen angle
concepts.explain: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Relative to an acute angle θ, the opposite side is across from θ and the adjacent side touches θ but is not the hypotenuse.

visual.caption: For the marked angle θ: opposite=3, adjacent=4 and hypotenuse=5.

steps: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{4}{5}$.
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\dfrac{3}{4}$. The ratios stay the same in a similar triangle.

practice.prompt: Opposite=5 and hypotenuse=13. What is sin θ?
Opposite=6 and adjacent=8. What is tan θ?

concepts.remember: These side-ratio definitions apply to the acute angles of a right triangle.
teaching: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side. Choose another angle: its opposite side faces it, and its adjacent leg touches it. Opposite and adjacent change when you choose the other acute angle.

Sine is opposite divided by hypotenuse; cosine is adjacent divided by hypotenuse; tangent is opposite divided by adjacent. In a 3–4–5 triangle with opposite side 3, these are 3/5, 4/5 and 3/4. Label sides before selecting the ratio involving your known and unknown lengths.

test.prompt: Scale factor from a 4 cm side to its corresponding 10 cm side?
test.solution: Divide the new length by the corresponding original length: 10/4=2.5.

test.prompt: Length scale factor 4 gives area factor?
test.solution: Area changes in two dimensions, so square the length scale factor: 4²=16.

test.prompt: Opposite=8 and hypotenuse=17. Find sin θ.
test.solution: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.

test.prompt: Adjacent=12 and hypotenuse=13. Find cos θ.
test.solution: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$.

test.prompt: Opposite=9 and adjacent=12. Find tan θ.
test.solution: Tangent is opposite divided by adjacent. Substitute and simplify: 9/12=3/4.

test.prompt: Similar triangles have corresponding sides 6 cm and 15 cm. A 4 cm side of the smaller triangle corresponds to how many cm in the larger?
test.solution: The length scale factor is 15/6=2.5. Multiply 4 by 2.5 to get 10 cm.

test.prompt: Two similar figures have length scale factor 5. What is the area scale factor?
test.solution: Area scales with the square of the length factor: 5²=25.

test.prompt: Opposite=7 and hypotenuse=25. Find sin θ.
test.solution: Use $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$=7/25.

test.prompt: Adjacent=8 and hypotenuse=17. Find cos θ.
test.solution: Use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$=8/17.

test.prompt: Opposite=12 and adjacent=5. Find tan θ.
test.solution: Use $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$=12/5.
